description: SFRA RAG Knowledge Base – v1, one block per major transformer fault type.

fault_knowledge.description: No significant abnormality detected in SFRA, energy bands, turbulence, HF decay or loss/efficiency profile.
typical_sfra_signatures: Smooth, repeatable frequency response with no unexpected peaks or notches.
Stable low-frequency region with expected resonances.
Mid-frequency patterns matching factory or historical baseline within tolerance.
High-frequency band without sudden deep notches or collapse.
supporting_observables: Loss and efficiency values within manufacturer limits.
No unusual vibration or acoustic noise.
DGA results without abnormal gassing trend.
Normal load and temperature behavior.

NONE.name: No Fault
NONE.summary: All rule-based thresholds lie in the healthy range; deviations remain within expected tolerance bands.
recommended_actions: Store this SFRA as a reference baseline if not already present.
Continue routine condition monitoring as per maintenance schedule.
Use trend analysis rather than single-shot decisions.
NONE.risk: No immediate risk indicated by current SFRA and calculated features.

recommended_tests: Periodic SFRA re-test based on criticality and utility policy.
Standard oil tests and DGA as per schedule.
Thermal and loading trend review.
preventive_actions: Maintain proper transport and handling procedures.
Avoid overloading and excessive through-faults.
Keep records of all SFRA traces for long-term trending.

fault_knowledge.description: Global mechanical distortion of winding geometry affecting inductance, capacitance and leakage reactance, leading to broad changes in SFRA signatures.
typical_sfra_signatures: Broad shift of resonant peaks across low, mid and high frequency regions.
Collapse or smearing of distinct resonances into wider, less-defined humps.
Significant deviation from baseline across a wide frequency band.
Asymmetry between phases for identical test configurations.
supporting_observables: History of through-faults or short-circuit events.
Transport or handling shocks without proper bracing.
Increase in leakage reactance compared to nameplate or baseline.
Abnormal vibration or noise under load.
common_root_causes: Severe short-circuit mechanical forces exceeding design withstand levels.
Improper clamping or loss of clamping force over time.
Transport without locking devices or inadequate bracing.
Aging and shrinkage of solid insulation allowing windings to move.

S1.name: S1 – Very Mild Deformation
S1.summary: Small SFRA deviations and minor modal shifts; pattern still broadly resembles baseline.
recommended_actions: Flag the unit for closer SFRA trend monitoring.
Cross-check with load current, temperature and basic electrical tests.
S1.risk: Low immediate risk but can be an early indicator of mechanical weakness.

S2.name: S2 – Mild Deformation
S2.summary: Clear but limited shifts in specific frequency bands; still acceptable for operation.
recommended_actions: Schedule detailed SFRA comparison of all phases and similar units.
Combine with DGA, insulation and capacitance/inductance checks.
S2.risk: Moderate risk if left unchecked; deformation can progress with future short-circuits.

S3.name: S3 – Moderate Deformation
S3.summary: Significant deviation from baseline in multiple bands; distinct resonances shifted or collapsed.
recommended_actions: Plan controlled outage for internal inspection where feasible.
Check mechanical clamping, spacers, blocks and winding support systems.
S3.risk: Elevated risk of further mechanical damage under future faults; reliability compromised.

S4.name: S4 – Severe Deformation
S4.summary: Major disruption in SFRA pattern; strong phase-to-phase mismatch.
recommended_actions: Avoid heavy loading and new short-circuit duty.
Perform thorough internal inspection and dimensional checks of windings.
S4.risk: High likelihood of failure during future mechanical stresses.

S5.name: S5 – Critical / Catastrophic Deformation
S5.summary: SFRA indicates collapse of characteristic structure consistent with major winding displacement.
recommended_actions: Remove the transformer from service as soon as practical.
Assess rewinding or replacement; do not return to normal service without remediation.
S5.risk: Very high risk of catastrophic failure; continued operation is not recommended.

recommended_tests: Phase-wise SFRA comparison including HV/LV, open/short configurations.
Impedance and leakage reactance comparison to nameplate and historical values.
Dissolved gas analysis for evidence of severe mechanical or thermal events.
Capacitance and inductance measurements for phase imbalance.
preventive_actions: Enforce mechanical bracing and locking procedures during transport.
Limit short-circuit exposure through network protection coordination.
Perform SFRA immediately after major faults and compare with baseline.
Maintain clamping systems and monitor for loosening over long-term operation.

fault_knowledge.description: Inward or outward buckling and distortion of windings in the radial direction due to hoop stresses.
typical_sfra_signatures: Pronounced changes in mid-frequency resonances associated with radial geometry.
Loss or shift of peaks linked to series inductance and radial spacing.
Asymmetry between phases for the same connection and test configuration.
In severe cases, collapse of a group of resonances in the mid band.
supporting_observables: History of heavy short-circuit currents close to the unit.
Change in short-circuit impedance beyond tolerance.
Uneven mechanical noise from specific limbs or phases.
High fault current duty in recent years without mechanical verification.
common_root_causes: High radial forces during external short-circuits.
Insufficient radial bracing or spacer design.
Aging and creep of solid insulation that reduces mechanical support.
Design not fully matched to actual network fault levels.

S1.name: S1 – Early Radial Distortion
S1.summary: Minor mid-frequency shifts, within or close to acceptance tolerances.
recommended_actions: Trend SFRA over time and after subsequent faults.
Re-check short-circuit impedance vs factory data.
S1.risk: Low, but indicates start of radial stress history.

S2.name: S2 – Mild Radial Deformation
S2.summary: Clear deviation from baseline in limited mid-frequency ranges; geometry still mostly intact.
recommended_actions: Increase SFRA monitoring frequency.
Assess loading and fault duty; derate if justified.
S2.risk: Possibility of progression during future short-circuits.

S3.name: S3 – Moderate Buckling
S3.summary: Distinct change in multiple mid-frequency resonances; pattern consistent with partial buckling.
recommended_actions: Discuss with OEM for structural assessment of windings.
Plan controlled outage for visual/mechanical inspection where practical.
S3.risk: Elevated risk that another short-circuit could cause severe mechanical damage.

S4.name: S4 – Severe Radial Collapse
S4.summary: Large part of the mid-frequency structure distorted or collapsed; strong phase differences.
recommended_actions: Consider the unit mechanically compromised.
Limit load and prepare to remove from critical duty.
S4.risk: High risk of failure under further mechanical stress.

S5.name: S5 – Critical Structural Collapse
S5.summary: SFRA indicates major radial failure; geometry no longer consistent with safe operation.
recommended_actions: Remove from service at earliest opportunity.
Decide on rewinding or replacement; do not return to normal duty without repair.
S5.risk: Very high risk of catastrophic failure if kept in service.

recommended_tests: Detailed SFRA around mid-frequency region for all phases.
Short-circuit impedance comparison test.
DGA for evidence of severe mechanical stress or arcing.
Visual inspection of windings and spacers when tank is opened.
preventive_actions: Design and verify radial bracing for actual network fault currents.
Avoid repeated high-magnitude through-faults.
Immediately test SFRA after major faults and compare against factory traces.
Implement stricter protection settings where possible.

fault_knowledge.description: Vertical upward or downward movement of windings along the limb axis, altering axial capacitance and inductance distribution.
typical_sfra_signatures: Low- and mid-frequency resonance shifts along the frequency axis.
Appearance of new resonances or disappearance of previously distinct peaks.
Differences between tap positions that were previously aligned.
Phase-to-phase mismatch indicating movement of one winding stack relative to others.
supporting_observables: Evidence of transport events without proper clamping or locking.
History of heavy through-faults or axial force events.
Unusual vibration profile along tank height.
Change in no-load current or excitation characteristics.
common_root_causes: Axial forces during short-circuits exceeding clamp capability.
Loss of end-block compression and axial wedges.
Shrinkage or creep in axial insulation packs.
Improper assembly or reassembly after repair.

S1.name: S1 – Minor Axial Shift
S1.summary: Small frequency shift of one or two resonances; still near baseline.
recommended_actions: Monitor SFRA trend on same limb and phase over time.
Check transport and operating history for mechanical incidents.

S2.name: S2 – Mild Axial Displacement
S2.summary: Multiple resonances slightly shifted; pattern broadly intact but clearly changed.
recommended_actions: Increase monitoring frequency and combine with other diagnostic tests.
Review clamping system design and previous maintenance records.
S2.risk: Moderate long-term risk if displacement continues.

S3.name: S3 – Moderate Axial Movement
S3.summary: Pronounced shift of several resonances; SFRA clearly inconsistent with baseline on one or more limbs.
recommended_actions: Plan outage for internal inspection of end-blocks and axial clamping.
Re-tighten or rebuild axial support structures as needed.
S3.risk: Elevated risk of dielectric stress and further mechanical deterioration.

S4.name: S4 – Severe Axial Displacement
S4.summary: Large axial shift; resonances may merge or disappear; phase-to-phase alignment is lost.
recommended_actions: Treat the unit as mechanically at-risk.
Avoid high load and severe network events.
Carry out mechanical overhaul of affected windings.
S4.risk: High risk of failure during future transients or faults.

S5.name: S5 – Critical Axial Misalignment
S5.summary: Response consistent with major displacement; possible partial short or dielectric clearance violation.
recommended_actions: Remove unit from critical service immediately.
Perform detailed mechanical and dielectric clearance assessment.
S5.risk: Very high risk of internal failure if operated without correction.

recommended_tests: Vertical vibration and acoustic survey along tank height.
SFRA comparison of multiple tap positions on the same phase.
Capacitance and inductance balance tests between phases.
Inspection of end blocks, wedges and axial clamping at outage.
preventive_actions: Use robust axial clamping systems and maintain bolt torques.
Inspect axial supports after major fault events.
Avoid frequent heavy through-faults by network coordination.
Include axial movement checks in factory and post-transport tests.

fault_knowledge.description: Multiple or unintended core-to-ground connections causing circulating currents, extra losses and local overheating.
typical_sfra_signatures: Changes in very low frequency region linked to core and grounding path.
Altered first resonances due to modified core-ground capacitance.
Differences between test configurations involving core or tank reference.
Subtle changes that correlate with other evidence such as losses and current.
supporting_observables: Increased core losses compared to factory data.
Higher than expected no-load current.
Localized hot spots on core or tank detected by thermal imaging.
Evidence from core insulation resistance tests or flux measurements.
common_root_causes: Degradation of core insulation packs or barriers.
Metallic debris bridging core to grounded structures.
Incorrectly installed or damaged core grounding leads.
Aging, moisture or thermal cycling weakening insulation.

S1.name: S1 – Suspected Core Grounding
S1.summary: SFRA and losses hint at possible additional ground path, but evidence is still weak.
recommended_actions: Repeat tests and confirm repeatability of signatures.
Perform core insulation resistance and flux-neutral tests.
S1.risk: Low to moderate; can evolve slowly but may cause long-term damage.

S2.name: S2 – Confirmed Additional Ground Path
S2.summary: Correlated evidence indicates more than one core ground point.
recommended_actions: Plan outage to localize and clear unwanted ground paths.
Inspect for metallic debris, damaged insulation or incorrect earthing connections.
S2.risk: Moderate; associated with increased losses and localized heating.

S3.name: S3 – Significant Core Grounding Fault
S3.summary: Core and tank behavior strongly affected; losses and temperatures elevated.
recommended_actions: Take unit under close loading control and plan corrective outage promptly.
Carry out detailed core inspection, cleaning and insulation repair.
S3.risk: High risk of progressive insulation damage if left unresolved.

S4.name: S4 – Severe Grounding with Hot Spots
S4.summary: Evidence of hot spots and severe loss increase; marked core behavior change.
recommended_actions: Avoid heavy loading and long-duration operation until issue is cleared.
Perform urgent internal inspection focusing on core clamps, bolts and insulation barriers.
S4.risk: High; thermal and mechanical deterioration can accelerate.

S5.name: S5 – Critical Core Ground Fault
S5.summary: Core grounding state considered unsafe for continued operation.
recommended_actions: De-energize the transformer as soon as practical.
Undertake full core inspection and rebuild where needed.
S5.risk: Very high; possible insulation breakdown or severe overheating if kept online.

recommended_tests: Core insulation resistance and core grounding continuity tests.
No-load loss and current measurement versus factory values.
Thermal imaging of core and tank areas.
SFRA in configurations sensitive to core-ground capacitances.
preventive_actions: Maintain cleanliness to avoid conductive debris inside tank.
Preserve integrity of key insulation pieces and barriers around core.
Verify core grounding layout after any major repair or retrofit.
Limit moisture ingress and aggressive thermal cycling.

fault_knowledge.description: Loss of mechanical tightness in core laminations, clamps, yokes, tie plates and frame assemblies, leading to vibration, noise and altered low-frequency behavior.
typical_sfra_signatures: Pronounced changes in very low frequency region (roughly 20 Hz – 1 kHz).
Suppression or broadening of first core-related resonances.
LF ripple or modulation of the curve due to vibrating laminations.
Deviation from baseline primarily in the lowest band with more stable higher-frequency regions.
supporting_observables: Increase in audible hum and mechanical vibration at 50/60 Hz and its harmonics.
Rise in magnetizing current compared to historical values.
Higher core losses and possible localized heating near clamps.
History of shocks, transport events or long-term aging without re-tightening.
common_root_causes: Loss of clamp bolt torque due to creep, relaxation or thermal cycling.
Pressboard shrinkage reducing compression on laminations.
Mechanical shocks during transport or seismic events.
Corrosion or wear of clamp and frame interfaces.

S1.name: S1 – Early Stage Loosening
S1.summary: Minor LF deviation and slight increase in hum or vibration; magnetizing current near normal.
recommended_actions: Trend SFRA and vibration over time.
Check accessible external clamps and supports for tightening.
S1.risk: Low immediate risk but can progress if left unchecked.

S2.name: S2 – Light Core Loosening
S2.summary: LF deviation more noticeable, audible noise; magnetizing current elevated.
recommended_actions: Plan maintenance window to inspect and re-tighten clamps where accessible.
Combine SFRA with vibration and acoustic analysis to localize loose regions.
S2.risk: Moderate; prolonged operation may accelerate insulation wear and losses.

S3.name: S3 – Moderate Loosening
S3.summary: LF deviation significant with clear ripple; magnetizing current and vibration clearly increased.
recommended_actions: Schedule outage to inspect internal core clamping, yoke clamps and tie plates.
Re-establish proper compression and replace damaged insulation packers.
S3.risk: Elevated; risk of lamination wear, burrs and local overheating increases.

S4.name: S4 – Severe Core Loosening
S4.summary: LF region heavily distorted; high vibration and hum; magnetizing current much higher than normal.
recommended_actions: Treat the unit as mechanically compromised.
Restrict load and avoid high fault duty until corrective work is done.
S4.risk: High; potential for evolving into core grounding faults or serious hot spots.

S5.name: S5 – Critical Core Instability
S5.summary: LF region highly distorted or collapsed; severe vibration and noise, high magnetizing current and loss.
recommended_actions: Consider de-energizing the transformer as soon as feasible.
Perform comprehensive core rebuild or re-stacking if necessary.
S5.risk: Very high; continued operation risks severe internal damage and potential failure.

recommended_tests: Focused SFRA on 20 Hz – 1 kHz region, compared against baseline.
Magnetizing current and core loss measurement at rated voltage.
Vibration and acoustic analysis on tank and core clamp regions.
Thermographic scanning for localized hot spots around core clamps.
preventive_actions: Verify and maintain core clamp bolt torque as per OEM guidance.
Minimize shocks during transport; use proper bracing.
Avoid extended operation under conditions that cause excessive vibration.
Perform periodic SFRA and vibration checks on aging units.

fault_knowledge.description: Localized shorted turns or severely weakened insulation between adjacent turns in a winding, causing highly localized changes in impedance and loss, often with thermal and dielectric stress concentration.
typical_sfra_signatures: Localized deep notches or sharp changes in the mid- to high-frequency bands.
Peak splitting or creation of additional resonances in a narrow frequency zone.
Phase-to-phase asymmetry where only one phase shows a pronounced high-frequency anomaly.
In severe stages, broader collapse of HF pattern where multiple resonances are damped or vanish.
supporting_observables: DGA showing increases in fault gases associated with arcing or severe partial discharge.
Elevated local winding temperature or hotspot indications from thermal monitoring.
Abnormal leakage current, partial discharge activity or failed insulation tests.
History of severe transient events such as lightning, switching surges or temporary overvoltages.
common_root_causes: Localized insulation deterioration between turns due to thermal aging or overloading.
Manufacturing defects such as insufficient spacing or sharp edges on conductors.
Contamination, moisture or particles causing bridging between adjacent turns.
Previous transient overvoltage that initiated partial turn breakdown.
Repeated short-circuit stresses weakening turn-to-turn insulation over time.

S1.name: S1 – Suspicious High-Frequency Anomaly
S1.summary: Minor HF notch or peak distortion observed in SFRA without strong corroborating evidence from other diagnostics.
recommended_actions: Repeat SFRA with consistent test setup to confirm the anomaly is stable.
Compare with historical and factory baseline curves for the same phase and configuration.
S1.risk: Low to moderate; could represent incipient turn insulation weakness or benign variation.

S2.name: S2 – Possible Incipient Inter-Turn Weakness
S2.summary: HF anomalies are repeatable and more clearly defined; other evidence supports emerging insulation stress.
recommended_actions: Increase monitoring frequency: SFRA, DGA and thermal measurements.
Review loading history, through-fault records and transient events.
S2.risk: Moderate; if not managed, defect can evolve into a true inter-turn fault.

S3.name: S3 – Localized Inter-Turn Fault Likely
S3.summary: SFRA shows clear, narrow-band HF notches or peak splitting with correlated abnormal gas trends.
recommended_actions: Plan a controlled outage for deeper diagnostic investigation.
Perform detailed insulation testing and engage OEM or specialist.
S3.risk: High; defect may progress under load, leading to rapid winding damage if stressed further.

S4.name: S4 – Significant Inter-Turn Fault
S4.summary: Multiple HF anomalies with strong supporting evidence from DGA and insulation tests; localized overheating likely.
recommended_actions: Restrict loading and avoid high short-circuit duty or emergency overloads.
Prepare for planned outage and internal inspection of the affected winding section.
S4.risk: High; continued operation poses substantial risk of rapid deterioration.

S5.name: S5 – Critical Inter-Turn Failure
S5.summary: Diagnostics strongly indicate active inter-turn fault with significant impact on local losses and dielectric integrity.
recommended_actions: Consider immediate de-energization if system conditions permit.
Plan for rewinding or replacement of the affected winding before returning to service.
S5.risk: Very high; serious risk of catastrophic winding failure and collateral equipment damage.

recommended_tests: High-frequency SFRA with close comparison across phases and test configurations.
DGA with focus on arcing-related gases and trending over time.
Partial discharge measurements where possible to localize activity.
Capacitance, inductance and insulation resistance tests across the suspected winding.
preventive_actions: Control loading to avoid repeated thermal over-stressing of windings.
Ensure lightning and surge protection schemes are adequate and maintained.
Maintain oil quality and dryness to improve dielectric withstand.
Use SFRA and DGA routinely after major faults or transient events.

fault_knowledge.description: Overall deterioration of solid and liquid insulation system, including paper, pressboard, oil and interfaces, leading to reduced dielectric margins and increased probability of partial discharge and breakdown.
typical_sfra_signatures: General softening or damping of multiple resonances across mid- and high-frequency ranges.
Less pronounced high-frequency structure compared to baseline, with peaks becoming smoother.
Subtle but consistent deviations across all phases rather than a single localized anomaly.
In advanced stages, collapse of high-frequency detail as dielectric properties change significantly.
supporting_observables: DGA showing progressive aging signatures and possible partial discharge indicators.
High moisture content in oil and paper, poor breakdown voltage and high dissipation factor.
Low degree of polymerization values indicating advanced paper aging.
Elevated temperatures during operation relative to historical behavior.
common_root_causes: Long-term thermal aging from continuous high loading or hotspots.
Inadequate drying and oil treatment leading to persistent moisture.
Ingress of oxygen and contaminants due to leaks or poor sealing.
Repeated overloading beyond nameplate rating.

S1.name: S1 – Early Insulation Aging
S1.summary: Minor SFRA changes with mild supporting evidence from oil tests; insulation still broadly acceptable.
recommended_actions: Increase frequency of routine oil and insulation testing.
Monitor SFRA trends and compare against similar units and baselines.
S1.risk: Low; aging is present but does not yet significantly compromise dielectric margins.

S2.name: S2 – Mild Degradation
S2.summary: SFRA deviations more noticeable in high-frequency bands; aging indicators above ideal values.
recommended_actions: Plan enhanced conditioning: oil filtration, drying and moisture control.
Restrict sustained overloading and closely monitor hottest-spot temperatures.
S2.risk: Moderate; continued stress may accelerate aging and reduce remaining life.

S3.name: S3 – Significant Insulation Degradation
S3.summary: SFRA shows clear damping of several resonances; diagnostics confirm reduced dielectric quality.
recommended_actions: Develop a life-management plan including possible derating of the transformer.
Consider intensive refurbishment such as oil reclamation and enhanced drying.
S3.risk: Elevated; dielectric margins are reduced and risk of insulation breakdown grows with stress.

S4.name: S4 – Severe Degradation
S4.summary: Multiple tools confirm advanced deterioration; SFRA high-frequency detail largely damped.
recommended_actions: Treat unit as high-risk asset and prioritize for refurbishment or replacement.
Significantly restrict overload and emergency duty.
S4.risk: High; risk of dielectric failure under normal or slightly elevated stresses is substantial.

S5.name: S5 – End-of-Life Insulation Condition
S5.summary: Insulation system considered near end-of-life; diagnostics show extensive deterioration.
recommended_actions: Schedule replacement or major refurbishment as a priority.
If left in service temporarily, use strict limits and continuous monitoring.
S5.risk: Very high; probability of major insulation failure is significant.

recommended_tests: Comprehensive oil quality analysis including moisture, breakdown voltage and dissipation factor.
DGA trending focused on aging and partial discharge-related gases.
Paper degree-of-polymerization testing where possible or indirect insulation health estimation.
SFRA trending over time and comparison with similar units.
preventive_actions: Maintain effective drying and oil treatment programs.
Avoid chronic overloading and operate within thermal design limits.
Ensure tightness of tank and bushings to prevent moisture ingress.
Apply timely refurbishment such as oil reclamation to slow further aging.

fault_knowledge.description: Loose mechanical components such as clamps, leads, connectors, support structures or non-core elements that introduce vibration, noise and localized stress without necessarily appearing as a classic core or winding fault.
typical_sfra_signatures: Subtle variations in SFRA curves that may change slightly with repeated tests or mechanical state.
Small distortions or ripples superimposed on otherwise normal responses.
Phase differences or configuration-dependent anomalies that correlate with certain mechanical positions.
supporting_observables: Observable rattling, knocking or intermittent mechanical noise during operation.
Changes in sound signature with load, tap position or cooling mode.
Vibration measurements showing localized peaks at specific frequencies or locations.
Visual signs of loosened hardware, supports or cable bracing when accessible.
common_root_causes: Insufficient tightening of external clamps, connections or supports.
Thermal cycling causing loosening of hardware over time.
Vibration due to cooling fans, pumps or external sources not properly damped.
Improper reassembly after maintenance or repair.

S1.name: S1 – Minor Mechanical Looseness
S1.summary: Very subtle indications with minor or no SFRA impact; mostly observed via sound or vibration.
recommended_actions: Inspect accessible external connections, clamps and structures.
Tighten or secure loose hardware following OEM torque specifications.
S1.risk: Low; primary concern is discomfort, minor stress and potential progression if ignored.

S2.name: S2 – Mild Looseness with Local Impact
S2.summary: Looseness affects localized areas such as leads or external busbars; SFRA impact limited or subtle.
recommended_actions: Localize the source through vibration and acoustic surveys.
Secure and brace leads, connectors and supports.
S2.risk: Moderate; may concentrate mechanical stress and contribute to long-term insulation wear.

S3.name: S3 – Significant Mechanical Looseness
S3.summary: Clear mechanical instability; SFRA may show configuration-dependent variations.
recommended_actions: Plan outage to inspect internal and inaccessible mechanical supports where possible.
Tighten and replace hardware, install additional bracing or damping where needed.
S3.risk: Elevated; risk of fatigue, conductor movement and localized insulation damage increases.

S4.name: S4 – Severe Looseness with Structural Concern
S4.summary: Mechanical components significantly unstable; risk of damage to conductors or insulation is high.
recommended_actions: Treat unit as mechanically at-risk; restrict loading if necessary.
Perform detailed inspection and corrective work including hardware replacement.
S4.risk: High; can contribute to electrical faults or collateral damage if not corrected.

S5.name: S5 – Critical Mechanical Instability
S5.summary: Severe mechanical looseness that may result in conductor failure, flashover or severe internal damage.
recommended_actions: Consider immediate removal from service if instability is confirmed.
Carry out urgent internal and external mechanical repair or reconstruction.
S5.risk: Very high; strong potential for sudden failure under normal or disturbed operation.

recommended_tests: Detailed vibration and acoustic analysis at multiple operating points.
SFRA before and after mechanical tightening to assess impact.
Thermal imaging of suspected loose connections or high-resistance joints.
Torque verification of critical bolted joints and clamps.
preventive_actions: Implement regular mechanical inspection and torque checks on critical fasteners.
Use proper bracing and damping for leads, connections and external conductors.
Inspect after transport, seismic events or significant mechanical shocks.
Monitor vibration trends and investigate any new or changing noise patterns.

fault_knowledge.description: Cumulative or single-event mechanical damage due to short-circuit forces, which may manifest as a combination of winding deformation, buckling, displacement and structural strain.
typical_sfra_signatures: Wide-ranging SFRA deviations that cannot be attributed to a single localized mechanism.
Combination of radial and axial pattern changes: peak shifts, collapses and altered resonances across several bands.
Phase-to-phase differences reflecting unequal stress or damage on individual limbs.
Significant deviation from factory or pre-fault SFRA baseline after a known severe fault event.
supporting_observables: Documented history of one or more high-magnitude short-circuit events close to the transformer.
Changes in short-circuit impedance measurements compared to factory data.
DGA evidence of severe mechanical or electrical stress during the incident.
Visible mechanical issues such as bent leads or shifted structures where accessible.
common_root_causes: External short-circuits exceeding design withstand levels.
Multiple high-energy faults over the service life without subsequent mechanical verification.
Protection miscoordination leading to prolonged fault duration.
Insufficient mechanical design margin relative to actual network fault levels.

S1.name: S1 – Minor Stress Signatures Post-Fault
S1.summary: Small SFRA differences detected post-fault; changes near acceptance limits.
recommended_actions: Trend SFRA periodically and compare with pre-fault baselines.
Verify short-circuit impedance remains within tolerance.
S1.risk: Low to moderate; indicates exposure to stress but not yet clearly damaging.

S2.name: S2 – Mild Damage from Short-Circuit
S2.summary: More noticeable SFRA deviations in selected bands, suggesting limited impact.
recommended_actions: Increase monitoring and perform SFRA after any additional fault events.
Consider limiting fault duty by network or protection adjustments.
S2.risk: Moderate; further faults could push damage into dangerous territory.

S3.name: S3 – Significant Mechanical Damage from Fault
S3.summary: SFRA shows distinct pattern changes indicating deformation or displacement.
recommended_actions: Engage OEM or experts to evaluate mechanical condition and residual withstand level.
Plan outage for internal inspection where technically and economically justified.
S3.risk: Elevated; ability to withstand future short-circuits is reduced.

S4.name: S4 – Severe Stress-Related Damage
S4.summary: Extensive SFRA deviation with evidence of major structural impact.
recommended_actions: Treat transformer as compromised for future short-circuit events.
Develop contingency plans such as spare units or network reconfiguration.
S4.risk: High; another severe fault could cause catastrophic failure.

S5.name: S5 – Critical Post-Fault Condition
S5.summary: Combined evidence indicates transformer no longer safely withstands design-level faults.
recommended_actions: Remove or protect the unit from positions with high fault exposure.
Plan for replacement or major rebuild on priority basis.
S5.risk: Very high; probability of catastrophic failure under further short-circuit stress is significant.

recommended_tests: Baseline versus post-fault SFRA comparisons for all phases.
Short-circuit impedance tests compared to nameplate and historical values.
Comprehensive DGA after each severe fault event.
Mechanical inspection of windings, spacers and structural elements during outages.
preventive_actions: Coordinate system protection to limit fault magnitude and duration.
Avoid locating mechanically weaker or aged units at high fault level buses.
Perform SFRA immediately after major faults for early detection of damage.
Select transformers with adequate mechanical margins for actual network conditions.

fault_knowledge.description: Issues within the on-load tap changer assembly such as contact wear, poor switching performance, resistive bridging, mechanical misalignment or contamination.
typical_sfra_signatures: Differences in SFRA traces between tap positions that were historically similar.
Unexpected anomalies tied specifically to certain tap positions or tap ranges.
Asymmetry between phases when taps are nominally in the same position.
Configuration-dependent changes, especially in tests that include the tap winding path.
supporting_observables: OLTC operation problems such as slow or failed tap changes, abnormal sounds or blocked operations.
Evidence of contact wear or burning from OLTC inspection reports.
Rising contact resistance, overheating or gas generation in the OLTC compartment.
Abnormal relay operations or protection trips during tap change operations.
common_root_causes: Aging and erosion of OLTC contacts due to repeated switching under load.
Insufficient maintenance, inadequate contact pressure or misadjusted mechanisms.
Contamination or degradation of OLTC oil leading to carbon deposits and sludge.
Mechanical misalignment or wear in drive linkages, gears and selector mechanisms.

S1.name: S1 – Early OLTC Condition Issues
S1.summary: Minor, tap-position-specific SFRA variations with weak or no corroborating symptoms.
recommended_actions: Correlate SFRA changes with tap position and historical data.
Increase monitoring of OLTC operations and count of tap changes.
S1.risk: Low; early indication that OLTC may require closer attention.

S2.name: S2 – Mild OLTC Degradation
S2.summary: Consistent SFRA differences at certain tap positions alongside mild OLTC symptoms.
recommended_actions: Schedule maintenance window to inspect and service the OLTC.
Check contact wear, spring forces and mechanical alignment.
S2.risk: Moderate; risk of tap change failures or increased contact heating if ignored.

S3.name: S3 – Significant OLTC Fault Behavior
S3.summary: Clear SFRA anomalies plus noticeable OLTC issues such as mis-operations, heating or relay activity.
recommended_actions: Limit unnecessary tap changes and avoid operating known problematic positions.
Carry out detailed OLTC inspection, cleaning and component replacement as needed.
S3.risk: Elevated; increased chance of OLTC failure, arcing and possible transformer trip.

S4.name: S4 – Severe OLTC Degradation
S4.summary: Severe tap-dependent anomalies with evidence of contact burning or mechanical jamming.
recommended_actions: Treat OLTC as a high-risk component and plan urgent repair or retrofit.
Avoid stressful tap operations and configurations inducing high current through damaged contacts.
S4.risk: High; potential for OLTC failure leading to load loss or internal damage increases substantially.

S5.name: S5 – Critical OLTC Fault
S5.summary: OLTC considered unsafe to operate; strong evidence of severe contact or mechanical failure.
recommended_actions: Minimize or completely avoid OLTC operation until repaired.
Take transformer out of service if safe operation cannot be guaranteed.
S5.risk: Very high; significant chance of serious fault or failure during OLTC operation.

recommended_tests: Tap-position-resolved SFRA comparison across the full operating range.
Dynamic resistance measurement or contact resistance testing of OLTC paths.
OLTC oil sampling and analysis for carbon and degradation products.
Mechanical inspection of drive mechanisms, selectors and diverter switches.
preventive_actions: Follow OEM-recommended OLTC maintenance intervals and procedures.
Avoid excessive tap operations when not needed for system regulation.
Maintain OLTC oil quality and cleanliness.
Monitor tap position usage to prevent overusing certain contacts disproportionately.

fault_knowledge.description: Problems with fixed or de-energized tap selector positions, such as poor contact engagement, incorrect tap setting, contamination or mechanical misalignment.
typical_sfra_signatures: Differences in SFRA between nominally equivalent DETC positions when compared over time.
Persistent anomalies at a single fixed tap setting that are not present in other units of the same design.
Subtle changes in low- or mid-frequency regions related to altered effective turns ratio or connection quality.
Phase imbalance in responses when only one phase is affected by a poor DETC connection.
supporting_observables: Unexpected voltage ratio deviations or regulation issues at a fixed tap setting.
Elevated contact resistance or heating at DETC connection points.
Inspection reports noting worn, misaligned or contaminated DETC contacts.
Abnormal behavior observed after a tap change made during an outage.
common_root_causes: Improper contact engagement after a manual tap change with the transformer de-energized.
Aging, wear or contamination on DETC contacts and insulating parts.
Mechanical misalignment or incomplete locking of the selected tap position.
Lack of maintenance or incorrect procedures during previous tap operations.

S1.name: S1 – Minor DETC Irregularity
S1.summary: Small, tap-specific SFRA deviations; voltage regulation and operation appear normal.
recommended_actions: Note the anomaly and monitor SFRA if further tap changes are performed.
Verify that ratio measurements align with nameplate and system design.
S1.risk: Low; condition may remain stable but warrants attention at next maintenance opportunity.

S2.name: S2 – Mild DETC Contact or Setting Issue
S2.summary: Clear but limited SFRA and electrical deviations at the selected tap; basic operation still acceptable.
recommended_actions: Plan detailed inspection and cleaning of DETC contacts at the next outage.
Confirm mechanical locking and correct position of the tap mechanism.
S2.risk: Moderate; long-term operation with poor contact can cause local heating and degradation.

S3.name: S3 – Significant DETC Problem
S3.summary: Significant SFRA differences with measurable impact on voltage ratio or losses; contact condition likely poor.
recommended_actions: Prioritize maintenance to inspect and repair DETC components.
Consider changing to a nearby healthy tap position if acceptable operationally.
S3.risk: Elevated; risk of local overheating and progressive deterioration if not addressed.

S4.name: S4 – Severe DETC Degradation
S4.summary: Serious SFRA and electrical anomalies; contact or connection integrity is doubtful.
recommended_actions: Treat DETC as high-risk; plan urgent outage for repair or replacement of damaged parts.
Avoid operating at the affected tap setting if an alternative is possible.
S4.risk: High; possibility of insulation damage, arcing or failure at DETC connection points.

S5.name: S5 – Critical DETC Fault
S5.summary: DETC condition considered unsafe; clear risk of failure at the selected tap position.
recommended_actions: Avoid energizing the transformer at the compromised tap setting.
Undertake immediate repair or rebuild of DETC components.
S5.risk: Very high; potential for serious damage or outage if operated without correction.

recommended_tests: SFRA comparison across different DETC settings where data is available.
Ratio and phase-angle tests at the actual in-service tap position.
Contact resistance measurement across DETC connections during outages.
Visual inspection and cleaning of DETC components and insulating supports.
preventive_actions: Apply correct DETC tap-change procedures strictly with the transformer de-energized.
Perform periodic inspection, cleaning and torque checks during major outages.
Maintain documentation of tap position changes and associated test results.
Avoid unnecessary tap movements; only change when system conditions require.
